title: Locks on hearts
hook: do they not reflect on the Qur'an, or are there locks on their hearts (47:24)

segments.voice: Yesterday: help Him, and He helps you. To help Allah is to help His cause, and your line was feet made firm.

You can read a page and arrive at the bottom with no idea what was on it. Eyes moved. Mind was elsewhere. It happens with a contract, a textbook, an email from a boss. People do it with scripture too, sometimes beautifully: a flawless recitation, every vowel in place, and nothing reaching the heart. Surah Muhammad has a question about that, and a picture you can almost hear: a lock, clicking shut.

Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's translation: "Will they then not meditate on the Qur'an, or are there locks on the hearts?" The Arabic verb behind meditate is yatadabbarun; its noun is tadabbur. The root d-b-r means the back of something, what comes after. Lexicons explain tadabbur as looking at the end of a matter, thinking through where a thing leads. So it isn't just reading. It's following a verse past its last word: what does this ask of me, where does it lead, what changes if I mean it. The Qur'an asks for this more than once. Surah An-Nisa' asks the same question, will they not ponder the Qur'an. Surah Sad says the book was sent down, blessed, so that people would ponder its verses and those with understanding would take heed. Then the lock. The verse says locks, plural, on hearts, plural, and the Arabic adds a small word, aqfaluha, their locks, as if each heart has its own lock fitted to it. Commentators read it as a heart sealed by habit, pride or carelessness until nothing gets in. Some scholars treat the question as a mirror for believers, especially the ones who read often, not an accusation thrown at outsiders. A report in Sunan an-Nasa'i, from Abu Dharr, says the Prophet ﷺ once stood in prayer through a night repeating a single verse until morning. The point wasn't how far he got. It was how deep.
screen: `TADABBUR: FOLLOW A VERSE PAST ITS END.` · `D-B-R: THE BACK, WHAT COMES AFTER.` · `EACH HEART WITH ITS OWN LOCK.` · `ONE VERSE, ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Take today's verse, will they not meditate, or are there locks on the hearts, and say it slowly in your head. Then ask the three questions of tadabbur: what does it say, what does it ask of me, where does it lead if I mean it? Stay with whichever question opens something, and if you pray, you can ask for the lock to open.
Tadabbur. Pondering that follows a verse past its last word, from the root for what comes after, asked for in 47:24. Today's word.
Your line: unlock the heart. Every heart, the verse suggests, has a lock of its own. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Alongside recitation, some Muslims join tadabbur circles or read a few verses daily with a tafsir, pausing to ask what each verse asks of them; some repeat a single verse many times in night prayer.

chat.meaning: 47:24 asks: will they not ponder the Qur'an? Tadabbur is thinking through where a verse leads. The Prophet once repeated one verse all night.
